Suffrage. Suffrage is the right to vote in political elections, a fundamental aspect of democracy. The expansion of suffrage from property-owning white men to all adult citizens regardless of race or gender was one of the central struggles of American and world history, achieved through centuries of activism, reform, and violence in the United States.

In the United States, voting was initially restricted to white male property owners. Successive expansions included non-property-owning men in the early nineteenth century, African Americans following the Fifteenth Amendment in eighteen seventy, and women following the Nineteenth Amendment in nineteen twenty. The Civil Rights Movement of the nineteen fifties and sixties challenged racial disenfranchisement through tactics including sit-ins, Freedom Rides, and the Voting Rights Act of nineteen sixty-five, which outlawed literacy tests and other mechanisms that suppressed Black voter registration.

Women's suffrage took nearly a century of activism, from the eighteen forty-eight Seneca Falls Convention to the nineteen twenty ratification of the Nineteenth Amendment. The movement included figures like Susan B. Anthony, Elizabeth Cady Stanton, and Emmeline Pankhurst in Britain. Disenfranchisement of Black voters in the South was systematic after Reconstruction. Literacy tests, poll taxes, grandfather clauses, and violence including lynching and intimidation kept Black citizens from voting until the Voting Rights Act of nineteen sixty-five.

The Fifteenth Amendment in eighteen seventy prohibited racial discrimination in voting. The Nineteenth Amendment in nineteen twenty prohibited gender discrimination. The Voting Rights Act in nineteen sixty-five abolished literacy tests and authorized federal oversight of elections. Suffragettes, women advocating for voting rights, employed confrontational tactics including property destruction and hunger strikes, generating controversy while advancing the cause. Modern voting rights battles continue today with disputes over voter ID laws, gerrymandering, and ballot access reflecting ongoing tensions over who gets to vote and whose votes count.
